title: The Essential Role of Advanced Materials Characterization in Understanding Irradiation Effects in Structural Materials
content: The ever-increasing need for dependable, continuous, safe sources of low C energy has focused attention on both existing and advanced nuclear fission power systems. As operation is extended, it is important to be able to predict the performance of the structural materials. This requires knowledge of the specific changes in the materials induced by neutron irradiation. Empirical models for the behavior of low alloy steels and welds used in pressurized water reactors (PWRs) were developed in the 1970-80’s in several countries based on the results of surveillance-irradiated Charpy V-Notch specimen tests, which measure the energy absorbed by the specimen as a function of test temperature (T), to determine the 41 Joule ductile-to-brittle transition temperature (DBTT) and assess the shift in DBTT (ΔT41J) compared to the non-irradiated steel. In addition, the decrease in upper shelf energy due to irradiation (ΔUSE) is also used as a measure of irradiation-induced degradation. The particular model used in the US is contained in US NRC Regulatory Guide 1.99, Rev. 2. The major variables in this correlation were the neutron fluence, Cu and Ni contents. Extensive research programs have been conducted over the past 50+ years to study irradiation damage in steels and welds in order to understand how the material properties are affected and what are the physical changes in the microstructure induced by neutron irradiation. The irradiation damage in low alloy steels is of particular importance for the reactor pressure vessel of PWRs. With identification of the physical changes in the material, it is possible to develop a mechanistic understanding of the microstructural evolution due to neutron irradiation.
